extracted.intended_audience: students in news-writing courses / novice reporters
extracted.subtask_description: Exercises and practical assignments for composing and revising news stories (obituaries, fires, sports, society, weather, bulletins) and for evaluating reporter conduct. Intended to train student reporters in factual completeness, timeliness, tone, and ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obituary story: required factual elements
rubrics_metrics.description: From the following details write for a New York morning paper a story of the death of Tom Hilton: Time and place of death, yesterday at the New York hospital; age, 36; occupation, sexton at Christ Church on West Thirty-sixth Street; attending physician, Dr. Henry Adair; cause of death, swallowing false teeth while at breakfast with his wife yesterday; efforts to save him: Dr. Adair summoned immediately, incision made in throat, silver tube inserted to allow passage of air to the lungs, and operation later at hospital. Patient failed to rally after operation. Survivors: wife and two children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include all the listed factual elements (time/place/age/occupation/attending physician/cause/medical efforts/outcome/survivors). Write for a New York morning paper—use appropriate lead, clear chronology of the mishap and medical response, and concise factual style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incident/fire report: essential details to include
rubrics_metrics.description: From the following details write for a Chicago evening paper a story of the fire that destroyed the plant of the W. M. Welch Manufacturing Company ... Date, to-day, April 19, at 4:30 A.M.; location, 1516 Orleans Street, Chicago; cause of fire, supposedly crossed wires on second floor where fire started; loss $60,000 according to C. M. Holmes, Jr., manager of the scientific department; persons injured, one fireman slightly injured by falling glass; institutions whose diplomas were destroyed (list); lives endangered, five firemen who were climbing a ladder on the rear wall when it fell; insurance, amount not obtainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting an accident/fire include date/time, precise location, suspected cause, estimated monetary loss (with source), injuries, institutions or parties affected, any lives endangered, and insurance status. Attribute estimates/suspicions to named sources; indicate unknowns (e.g., insurance amount) rather than guessing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and fix weak points in a near-complete human-interest story
rubrics_metrics.description: The following almost excellent news article has one grave weakness. Rewrite the story, strengthening the weak points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose the story's principal flaw (missing lead, weak chronology, absent key facts, poor ending, unclear significance, or tone mismatch). Strengthen by adding/clarifying necessary facts, sharpening the lead, tightening chronology, and improving transitions while preserving factual material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt obituaries and local notices for a weekly paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct in any way needful the following stories for a weekly paper (examples provided: short death notices and a longer biographical death notice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor length, tone, and detail to a weekly audience: remove florid or cliché phrasing, clarify dates/places/cause, provide burial details (cemetery, service), correct grammar and chronology, and ensure the essential facts (relation, survivors, funeral arrangements) are present and readable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weather story: use forecasts and write current/tomorrow's prospects
rubrics_metrics.description: Get the local and state weather forecast and write for to-morrow morning's paper a story of to-day's weather and to-morrow's prospects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain official local and state forecasts (attributed). Report today's conditions succinctly and describe tomorrow's prospects, emphasizing impacts (commuting, events) and any warnings. Use timely, actionable phrasing suitable for a morning audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports story critique and rewrite: clarity, objectivity, key facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticize and rewrite the following baseball story (example contains florid, biased, and cliché-laden copy about the White Sox losing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove excessive sarcasm, clichés, and insulting language. Preserve and present scoreboard facts (final score), key plays, pivotal innings, pitcher changes, errors, and standout performances in clear chronological order. Use objective tone, attribute judgments, and avoid inventing metaphors that obscure facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment: cover athletic contests for next-day paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Take as a special assignment a local football, basketball, or baseball game, or some other athletic contest and report it for the following morning's paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be on-site, gather score, statistics, quotes from coaches/players, key moments, and context. File promptly for the morning edition, prioritizing an accurate lead and concise game narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Society/engagement/wedding story: required elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the story of the engagement/wedding for the society column (examples list parents, ages, occupations, addresses, officiant, attendants, gown/attire details, color scheme, number of invitations, luncheon details, honeymoon plans, future residence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include named participants (bride/groom/parents), ages, occupations/positions, residences/addresses, date/time/place of ceremony, officiant, attendants and their relations, attire details or heirlooms, color/flower scheme, invitation count, reception/luncheon details, honeymoon plans and future address; emphasize social significance but keep factual economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite rival morning stories for an afternoon edition (no new details)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite for this afternoon's paper the two following stories appearing in rival publications this morning. No additional details have been obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with only the available material—do not invent facts. Produce a concise, fresh version suitable for the afternoon deadline: tighten lead, remove repetition, reorganize chronology, and possibly emphasize a different angle for timeliness while attributing original sources where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate late bulletins into prior coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection (i) below is a bulletin received some hours after the news detailed in (2) ... Combine the bulletin with the morning story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a bulletin arrives after an earlier dispatch, merge the new facts into the narrative: update the lead if necessary, add the new development with proper time stamps and attribution, and preserve earlier verified details. Ensure the combined story reads cohesively and clarifies sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify sources; beware of fabricated interviews and 'verisimilitude' tricks
rubrics_metrics.description: A rival paper's young men routinely printed travelers' tall tales and corroborated them with hotel-register names and complicit clerks; the Tribune reporter failed to find these nonexistent explorers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify interviews and travelogues independently. Do not accept uncorroborated claimant narratives; corroborative details (hotel registers, named witnesses) must be checked for authenticity. Avoid relying on competitors' colorful but unverified copy; use skepticism and attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate reporter conduct and newsworthiness (doorstepping/privacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mrs. Laura Paltier 'not at home' anecdote: reporters sought to ask about a $20,000 exposition fund; the maid repeatedly told reporters she was 'not at home.' Question: Do you find the story meritorious or blameworthy? Why?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess newsworthiness vs. intrusion: consider public interest (fund responsibility) and privacy. Judge reporter persistence (doorway/telephone) against standards of respectful inquiry and source availability; report ethically—note refusals, attempt alternate contacts, and explain relevance to readers rather than sensationalizing refusal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature reporting: collect statistics and human-source interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a feature on ways students make money: 'Get statistics of the number of students earning their way wholly or in part and the amount of money earned during a college year.' Also: 'Interview several ladies who have dimples and write the story' after an expert's technical remark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For features, gather quantitative data (counts, amounts, percentages) with sources and methods, and complement with multiple interviews to illustrate patterns. Attribute expert statements and seek corroborating viewpoints. Combine data and human detail for balanced, informative features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Death/mystery case reporting: document autopsy/police findings and physical evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting on Emily Benton: early reports include autopsy held in secret, no charges, bruise marks, mouth discoloration suggesting possible chemical, lack of struggle, found bottle nearby, coroner and sheriff involvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report coroner/autopsy findings and police actions carefully, attribute preliminary observations, describe physical evidence (bruises, chemicals, bottles) without asserting cause until official results, and avoid speculative language. Note information gaps and pending inquests.
